title: Between West and West by North
logline: Off a straight surf coast with no harbour, the only way to find the old anchorage was a bearing: put one hooded peak forty kilometres inland between west and west by north, and let go the anchor. In 1603 Dutch ships lay on that line while their vice-admiral and about fifty men were killed somewhere on the plain between, and the next morning a letter came down to the beach calling the killing God's justice. Every account of what happened was written on the ships' side. The film never leaves the line they looked along.
human_question: When the harm I do has a good name, justice, defence, what the other side deserved, does the name change the mind that did it?

place.what_kind_of_place: A line across a landscape rather than a spot on it. At one end, a long, straight, harbourless surf coast on the east of the island, where boats are pulled up on open sand and the only anchorage is wherever the seabed is fine sand at seven to nine fathoms. Behind the beach a thin strip of palms and low roofs, then a brackish backwater arm, then a plain of paddy so flat that a single tree reads as a landmark. At the other end, about forty kilometres inland, a granite peak of roughly 650 metres rises alone out of forest reserve, with a rounded cowl of a summit that seafarers named for a friar's hood. Between the two runs one compass bearing, a little north of west from the sea. The film keeps to that bearing and looks along it, one way or the other, in every shot.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because forty kilometres of flat country, seen end-on through a very long lens, collapses into layers: surf, palms, water, paddy, a band of haze, and above all of it the one hooded shape, as if cut from paper and stood up on the horizon. The peak is only there at the ends of the day; by mid-morning heat haze takes it and the plain has no horizon at all, and in the evening it comes back as a silhouette. On a few evenings a year, on this record's calculation, the sun seen from the old anchorage goes down exactly into it. From the summit the view reverses: the whole plain laid out in the first light and, at its far edge, the thin bright line of the sea where the ships lay.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The light and the air, almost nothing else. The peak appears, fades in the rising haze and reappears; the plain changes from blue to green to gold with the hour and the crop; the surf keeps its own time at the near end; cloud builds on the peak on some afternoons and caps it. At the payoff the sun lowers through haze toward the cowl, touches it and is gone behind it within a few minutes, and the whole line goes grey from the sea inland.
place.when_it_looks_best: The south-west monsoon months, roughly May to September, when this coast is in its dry season and the evenings are clearest; best of all the last days of August, when the sunset should line up with the peak from the anchorage (mid-April gives a second window, in a stormier season). Dawn for the summit, evening for the sea end. The middle of the day is filmed only to show the peak gone.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film held on one compass line. It opens high over the surf at the end of the day, looking inland along the bearing: sea, a thin fringe of palms, flat paddy to the horizon and one hooded peak standing on it. Then the same line from the middle of the plain in the morning, the peak dissolving into heat; the backwater at the edge of the fields gone still; the summit before sunrise looking back the other way at the whole plain and the sea's bright edge. It ends where it began, over the surf in the evening, with the sun going down exactly into the peak. Every shot is locked, every lens is long, and nothing is ever filmed off the line. Sound is surf at one end and wind at the other.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The line is how a Dutch sailor of 1603 wrote down where his ships anchored, and it is the only part of that summer's story that is still where the documents put it. On the first of June the vice-admiral Sebald de Weert and about fifty of his men were killed somewhere on the plain after meeting the king of the hill kingdom, Vimaladharmasuriya; the next morning a letter in Portuguese came down to the beach saying God had done justice. The voice lays the surviving accounts side by side, a merchant's, a sailor's, a chaplain's seventy years later, and shows that they cannot agree on the cause, the words, the drink, the numbers or even whether anyone urged the order, which is the one distinction the texts this series follows make between the two minds rooted in hate. What the texts do fix is the thing the letter claims an exception to: the hatred in killing an enemy who comes to harm you is, they say, that mind's fierce form, not its exemption. The film reads no one's mind, shows no killing and takes no side; it stands on the side every writer stood on, looking in from the sea.

sequence.on_screen: Late afternoon. The drone hangs still about a hundred metres over the surf line, facing inland on the bearing, long lens, locked: white water at the bottom of frame, a thin fringe of palms and low roofs, a plain so flat it has no features, and far off, pale above the haze, one hooded peak. Nothing moves but the surf. The sound is surf only.
sequence.voice: There is no harbour on this coast. In 1603 a Dutch sailor wrote down how to find the place to anchor: it is a dangerous shore, he said, and hard to see where the roadstead is, but there is a mountain inland; when it stands between west and west by north of you, you are there, in seven, eight or nine fathoms, on fine sand. That spring the ships of the vice-admiral Sebald de Weert lay on this line.

sequence.on_screen: Morning, from a raised field bund in the middle of the plain, on the same bearing. A very long lens stacks field on field, a line of palms, a single tree, and the peak faint behind them. Over two or three minutes, locked off, the heat haze rises and the peak thins and disappears, leaving a plain with no horizon.
sequence.voice: On the first of June about two hundred men came ashore with drums and banners and marched inland to meet the king of the hill kingdom, Vimaladharmasuriya, who had travelled down to the coast to see them and the Portuguese ships they had taken. By night the vice-admiral and about fifty of his men were dead. What happened in between exists only in writing, all of it Dutch, and none of it by anyone who was in the room.

sequence.on_screen: Midday, the same bund. The peak is gone. The camera holds on the shimmering plain, then cuts to three locked details on the bearing, each held long: a water channel running straight toward where the mountain was, a bund's edge, the haze itself. No people, no village.
sequence.voice: The accounts do not agree. A merchant in the fleet, Jan Harmensz Bree, has an invitation refused, first to the shore and then on board, and an answer that the ships would sail for home instead; then an order to bind the vice-admiral, and then to kill. He adds that many in the fleet put the cause earlier, in Portuguese prisoners the king had asked for and the Dutch had set free. A sailor, Jan Jacobsz Rycks, has drink passed round on both sides, hard words on both sides, and the king's own people pressing for the order. Seventy years later a Company chaplain, Philippus Baldaeus, has the drink on one side only, a remark about the queen, and three words: bind the dog.

sequence.on_screen: Late afternoon at the backwater arm between the fields and the coast strip, looking west along the bearing. The water is dead still and takes the whole sky; the peak returns as a grey shape and lies doubled in it. Locked; a heron may cross, nothing is staged.
sequence.voice: The texts this series follows divide the mind rooted in hate in only one way: whether it arises of itself, or after someone urges it. These accounts cannot settle even that. One has an order that follows an answer; one has men urging; the chaplain has a whisper in the king's ear. The texts count a killing done by one's own hand or through others. And read against their list of ordinary occasions for this mind, both sides of that day are on it: each had asked the other for something, and each had been refused.

sequence.on_screen: Next morning, first light, at the tideline itself: a locked wide frame of the empty beach and the surf, looking out to sea along the reverse of the bearing, toward where the ships lay. The sun comes up out of the water to one side of frame. Only the sound of the surf.
sequence.voice: The next morning an envoy came down to the beach under a white flag with a letter in Portuguese. As the merchant's diary gives it, it began: God yesterday executed right and justice, and this for reasons. A second letter said that God does justice to those who ask it of him and deserve it. The chaplain's version, printed seventy years on, begins differently: who drinks wine is not good. No letter survives in its own words; each is known only as the men it was sent to wrote it down.

sequence.on_screen: The far end of the line. On the summit of the peak before sunrise, the camera looks back east along the bearing: the plain in blue shadow, the backwater arm catching the first light, and at the very edge of the world the thin bright line of the sea. Locked; wind only. The sun rises to the left of the bearing.
sequence.voice: The texts make no exception for a name like justice. The shorter one says the hatred felt in killing an enemy who comes to do you harm is not another thing: it is the fierce form of the same one. The older one lists the faces this aversion wears, anger, fear that judges its object too strong and wants to be away from it, the wish for revenge, the wish to destroy, and offers none of them as excused. Whether turning down an invitation you distrust is itself one of those faces, the texts do not say, and this film does not decide.

sequence.on_screen: The payoff, back over the surf on the evening the sun lines up. The drone holds exactly where the film began, on the bearing, longest lens. The sun lowers through the haze, touches the cowl of the peak and goes down behind it; for a moment the mountain is a black hood with light round its edge. Then the whole line goes grey from the far end toward the sea. Hold until the surf is the only thing left to see.
sequence.voice: Nobody knows which room it happened in, or what was in anyone's mind there. No account from the king's side survives except letters quoted by the men who received them. What is still where the documents put it is this mountain, and the line the ships lay on. The texts do not ask who was right. They say that no killing is done with any other kind of mind, and that where you face an enemy is where that mind is fiercest, not where it stops.

concept_merge.why_together: C007 supplies the category the story's own document claims to stand outside: two hate-rooted minds, always with displeasure, differing only in whether they arise unurged or with urging [C007-P:L25–L28; C007-M:L3–L9], with killing, harsh speech and ill will fixed to them [C007-P:L53], killing done 'by one's own hand or through others' [C007-P:L59], and the flat refusal of any exception: the hatred in killing an enemy who comes to harm you is its fierce form [C007-M:L11]. Its list of everyday occasions, including when what one asks of others is not given, when one's word is not accepted, when others act as enemies and when one thinks others will do wrong [C007-M:L17], fits both parties of 1603 at once, which keeps the film from taking a side. C022 supplies the faces the same aversion wears, anger, fear as the aversion that judges its object strong and means to get away from it, the wish for revenge and the wish to destroy [C022-P:L121; C022-M:L35], and the distinction that stops the film calling any caution healthy or hateful: the fear the texts praise is dread of wrongdoing, a different factor [C022-P:L63].
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the texts' question about anger is not 'was it justified?' but 'what kind of mind was it?', and that a claim of justice, even one written in the claimant's own letter the next morning, is exactly the case they refuse to exempt [C007-M:L11]. It also shows how little the record can say about any mind: the accounts split on precisely the distinction the texts use, urged or unurged [C007-M:L9], and the digest's own open question whether an order given to others is the prompted mind at all [C007-P:L59] is left open. The film therefore places the charge on the document's claim and on the doctrine, never on a man.

concept_links.why: C007 needs a harmful act that arrives with a justification attached, because its sources make no exception for justified anger: Margaya says the hatred that arises in killing an enemy who comes to harm you is the fierce (raudra) form of the hate-rooted mind, just as killing for sport while laughing is its subtle form [C007-M:L11], and the digest's does_not_transfer rules out 'righteous anger' in those words. The 1603 killing is one of the very few events on the island where the justification survives as a document from the next morning: a letter, known only through the recipients' diaries, that begins 'God yesterday executed right and justice'. The texts fix killing, harsh speech and ill will to these minds [C007-P:L53] and count killing done 'by one's own hand or through others' [C007-P:L59], which is how every account has the order carried out. They split the two hate-rooted minds only by urging [C007-P:L25–L28; C007-M:L9], and the accounts disagree on precisely that, so the film shows the split and does not settle it. The occasions list [C007-M:L17] includes refusals on both sides. Guards from does_not_transfer: no 'venting' and no 'anger only hurts yourself' that would play down fifty deaths [C007-P:L47; C007-P:L53]; the bodily effects and the lower-realm claim are traditional teaching and are never narrated as fact [C007-P:L47; C007-P:L51], which rules out the chaplain's story of the king's burning fever; grief is classed with this mind [C007-M:L19; C007-P:L49], so no mourner and no remembrance appear.

C022 gives the list of faces this one aversion wears, anger, fear as the aversion that 'judges the disliked object strong and means to get away from it', dissatisfaction, the wish for revenge and the wish to destroy [C022-P:L121], with Margaya putting fear and anger under the same word [C022-M:L35]. The film uses it over the summit shot as doctrine, not as a reading of anyone: the king's letter gives as its reason that he would have been taken on board by force, and the digest's does_not_transfer warns that 'fear is healthy survival instinct' does not map onto the source, while the fear the texts praise is dread of wrongdoing, a different factor [C022-P:L63]. Exemption ruling: undecidable. Nothing in C022 says whether declining an invitation one distrusts is the aversion or ordinary prudence, and the voice says so rather than calling the refusal either fearful or wise.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the texts' account of the mind rooted in hate has no exception for a killing called justice or defence, and names the enemy who comes to harm you as that mind's fiercest occasion, not its excuse; that the only line the texts draw inside it is whether it was urged; that the historical record of one day in 1603 cannot even say which side of that line the order fell on, because every account was written by the other party, most of them absent and one seventy years late; and that the honest way to look at such a day is from where the writers stood, without claiming to see into the room.
what_must_be_real: The bearing, the peak and the light as they are. Every shot is genuinely taken on the stated line, and the sunset alignment is shot on the real evening it happens or not at all: no composite, no moved sun, no time-lapse passed off as one evening. No killing is shown, reconstructed, re-enacted or implied by sound; no engraving of the massacre or the reception is used, though both exist from 1605. No village, market, house of worship or person in the plain or on the coast strip is framed or identified; the towns are seen only as a thin band on the horizon of a long-lens frame. Quotations from the diaries and letters are read as given in their published English translation and attributed to their writer; no line is attributed to a source that does not contain it.
position_hint: In the anger-and-fear stage after the film that introduces the two hate-rooted minds on a written urging: this is the film that meets the objection every viewer brings, that some anger is justified, with the texts' refusal of that exception, before the group turns to suspicion, fear as retreat and remorse.
risks: Narrating a mental state. Every source attributes states: the 1604 summary and the merchant have the king 'enraged', the chaplain has him 'naturally a cholerick person' who 'dissembled his anger', and has de Weert 'heated with strong liquor'. None of these is quoted or paraphrased in the voice. The voice reports acts, words spoken or written, and who wrote them; it says outright that no one knows what was in anyone's mind.

Kamma as fate. Baldaeus follows the killing with the king's 'burning fever', his drinking from an ice-cold brook without relief, his death in misery in 1604, and the king's reported view that de Weert 'had no more than what he deserved'. The whole passage is recorded in historical_thread so it is not told halfway, but none of it enters the film: it reads as punishment, it echoes the traditional bodily effects the digest forbids narrating as fact [C007-P:L47; C007-P:L51], and 'deserved' is exactly the verdict the floor forbids.

Taking a side. The Dutch accounts excuse and accuse by turns (the merchant and the 1604 summary both record fleet opinion that the released prisoners were the real cause; the chaplain moves the drink to one side). The voice gives both sides' refusals [C007-M:L17] and gives no verdict on who broke faith. No 'treachery', 'murder' or 'massacre' in the voice; those are the sources' words and stay in the thread.

Playing down the harm. The texts' stress on the angry person's suffering must not become a slogan that shrinks fifty deaths [C007-P:L47; C007-P:L53]; the voice states the deaths plainly once and does not return to them as spectacle.

Bereavement and memorial register. The coast at the sea end was among the places struck by the 2004 tsunami and may carry memorials to it; none is framed and the tsunami is not mentioned. The 1603 dead are not mourned or memorialised in the voice; grief is classed with this mind in the source [C007-M:L19] and the film stays away from it.

Living communities and live disputes. The plain and coast strip are densely settled today, and the forest reserve round the peak is associated with the island's indigenous people. No community, town, religious building or person is framed or named, and the question of whose 'kingdom' the coast then belonged to (the sources speak of a local 'king' subject to the hill king) is not entered. The civil war and the district's later violence are out of bounds and never alluded to.

The alignment as a trick. The sun setting into the peak is a calculation from a rounded coordinate and must be verified; if it fails, the payoff is the peak's silhouette at sunset on the bearing, and the voice never claims the alignment means anything. It is a way to see the one fixed point, not a sign.

A repeated argument. IDEA-0033 already carries the prompted mind on a written urging. Here the urging is only one disputed layer, stated once and left open; the film's own demonstration is the refusal of the justified-anger exception [C007-M:L11], which no other film in the group carries.
drop_if: The peak cannot be seen from any practical position over or near the surf on the bearing (haze every evening of the window, or palms and buildings blocking a legal drone height); without the peak there is no line and no film.
Drone flight over the coast is refused and no boat position a kilometre or two offshore clears the palm line; the sea end then has no frame.

A primary-source check (Wieder's 1933 edition of the Spilbergen voyage, Commelin, or the Rycks manuscript) places the 1603 anchorage or the king's lodging somewhere other than the southern coast Ferguson identified; the bearing would then belong to a different shore.
Filming in the forest reserve is refused and no position on the plain's western edge gives the reverse view; the film can survive without the summit only if the sea end and the plain still carry it.

connections.note: The same district's coast, about seventy kilometres south: an open beach and roadstead where the sea is read from the sand at first light, a film about two honest readings of one swell. This film turns its back on the sea: its roadstead is only the platform for looking inland along a bearing, its subject is documents, not weather, and its payoff is a mountain at sunset.

The great backwater's upper reaches at night, lit only by hand lamps. This film was first proposed at that backwater's northern mouth; the 1603 sources call that mouth by another name and put the anchorage far to the south, so this film moved and never films the lamp country.

A lagoon bar filmed from height as a diagram of lagoon, bar and sea. The first proposal for this film ended on the same kind of frame; it was dropped for that reason as well as for the location, and this film has no bar shot.

A ruined monastic ridge in the same cluster of inland hills, filmed as light crossing it in the first and last minutes of the day. This film uses a different peak of the cluster only as a distant mark and, once, as a viewpoint back to the sea; it never films the ridge or any ruin.

The same group's film on a written urging to remove a man for a thought, which carries the prompted hate-rooted mind. Here the urging is only a disputed layer in the accounts, left open; this film's own argument is the texts' refusal of the justified-anger exception, set against a letter that claims it.

Proposed for the same group: an island seen only from a drifting boat under overcast, on suspicion of wrongs not yet done. Both films keep the camera outside; that one drifts and zooms and never arrives, this one is locked on a single compass bearing at the two ends of the day, with a celestial alignment as its payoff.

selection.reason: Carries C007's refusal of any exception for justified anger on a primary document that claims exactly that exception, a king's letter the morning after a killing saying God had done justice, and on four contemporary or near-contemporary accounts that disagree on the one distinction the texts draw, urged or unurged. The location was moved from the blind proposal's lagoon mouth, where the event did not happen, to the anchorage bearing the 1603 sources actually give, which also supplies the film's frames. Weaker than the best films on the slate because the spot of the killing is lost and the film must stand on a sightline.

review.note: The body of this record was replaced entirely on 2026-09-26 in the blind GRP-03 rework and rebuilt from fresh research; the previous body was not read. Under standing decision 9 the verdict is pending; the old status was also pending, so no confirmation or rejection has been reset. The concepts are unchanged (C007 primary, C022 supporting). The film and its title are new (the old title is kept in aliases). A blind colleague proposed the northern mouth of the great eastern backwater for the 1603 killing of the Dutch vice-admiral Sebald de Weert. Tested against the primary accounts in Donald Ferguson's annotated translations (1928), it failed: the 1603 town was not the later fort-town on the backwater but an older capital a few miles inland of the coast to the south, and the 1603 sources give that northern mouth a different name and put it some thirty miles from the anchorage. The proposal's payoff, a high static frame of a lagoon bar, also repeats IDEA-0147. The film moves to the anchorage the sources describe, found by a bearing on an inland peak, which moves it out of the proposal's district into its southern neighbour (5 to 6 films; the proposal's district stays at 4), as the research note sets out. Other corrections: the widely repeated '300 killed on the beach' is impossible on the primary counts (about 200 landed; 47 to 53 died); 'Bind the dog' and the drunken remark about the queen appear first in Baldaeus (1672), not in the 1603 diaries, one of which records drink on both sides and the other none; and the king's letter survives in two different wordings, neither of them the original. The treatment is a locked, long-lens film on one compass bearing, at sunset from over the surf and at dawn from the summit, paying off on the sun setting into the peak on a date still to be verified. Weakest points: no exact spot, a living town in the middle of the line that cannot be filmed, forest-reserve access to the summit unverified, and a sixth film in the district.

suggested_location.name: The 1603 roadstead of 'Matecalo' off Karaitivu, and the bearing inland across the Sammanthurai plain to Friar's Hood (Walimbe Hela / Valimbe Hela), the landmark the Dutch pilots anchored by

also_known_as.name: Matecalo / Matekeloe / Maetekeloo / Batecalou
also_known_as.meaning: the 1603 spellings of the place the Dutch visited; Ferguson identifies the town with present Sammanthurai

also_known_as.name: Hang Up
also_known_as.meaning: 'blubber-lip', the Dutch sailors' first name for the peak

also_known_as.name: Capello de Frade / Nunnikskap / Friar's Hood
also_known_as.meaning: friar's hood, from the shape of the summit
also_known_as.used_by: Portuguese, Dutch and British charts; Survey Department triangulation station

suggested_location.region: Ampara District, Eastern Province: the whole line lies in Ampara District, from the surf off Karaitivu on the east coast (the sea end), across the backwater arm and the paddy plain of Sammanthurai, to Friar's Hood in the Nuwaragala forest reserve in the Uhana division (the inland end), about 40 km on a bearing of roughly 279 degrees from the shore
suggested_location.why_here: Because this is where the 1603 killing of Sebald de Weert actually happened, and because the only way the sources locate it is a line the camera can stand on. The blind proposal put the story at the northern mouth of the Batticaloa lagoon, following modern retellings that say simply 'Batticaloa'. The primary accounts, as translated and annotated by Donald Ferguson (JCBRAS vol. XXXI, 1928), say otherwise: the Dutch ships lay in an open roadstead on a 'dangerous shore' where 'Matecalo lies a short mile inland', found by putting an inland mountain 'between west and west-by-north' (Rycks); the town was 'some full two miles inland' (Bree); Ferguson identifies it with present Sammanthurai, three or four English miles from the sea, the landing village perhaps with Karaitivu, the mountain with Friar's Hood, and the sources' 'river of Poligamme' with the northern entrance of the backwater, 28 to 30 miles from Karaitivu. A modern summary agrees that Sammanthurai was the region's capital until the Portuguese moved it to Puliyantivu in 1628. The spot of the killing is lost inside a living town the film cannot enter; the bearing is not. It is the one thing in the story still where the documents put it, and it gives the film a sea end, a plain and a 650 m peak on one line.

historical_thread.story: Sebald de Weert, vice-admiral of Wybrand van Warwijck's VOC fleet, first visited the east coast of Ceylon in November–December 1602 and went up to Kandy to treat with Vimaladharmasuriya I against the Portuguese. He returned from Aceh with seven ships and came 'into the road before Batacalou' on 25 April 1603. Between 16 and 23 May the ships took four Portuguese vessels. The king wrote asking, 'for God's sake', that the Portuguese not be released but delivered to him; de Weert had promised them their freedom and on 29 May released them with two ships and passports for Negapatam. The king came down to Matecalo. On 1 June about 200 men landed with drums and banners, met the king about half a mile beyond the town (Rycks has him with the 'king' of Matecalo and the 'king' of Panawa), and marched with him to Matecalo. The king asked that the men go back on board and return next day; de Weert stayed with 'some of the chief officials' (Bree) or 25 or 26 men (Rycks). The men went back to the shore in disorder, some staying in the town's taverns. After de Weert asked the king to come to the shore and on board, the king, as Bree gives it, answered that he had come from Kandy to Vintana and thirty miles further to Matecalo, and that this further request was 'not a little suspicious' to him; de Weert replied that if the king would not trust him so far, he would not go to Punto de Gallo but home. The king commanded the modeliar, 'a Portuguese by birth' (Ferguson: Manuel Dias), to bind the vice-admiral and afterwards to kill him and his companions, and stragglers on the way to the shore were attacked. Rycks instead has drink passed round, the vice-admiral intoxicated, the two falling to abusing each other, and the king's 'people, who incited him, so that he consented'; he alone adds the 'king' of Poligamme lying in the woods with 300 men told to kill any Dutch he could. On 2 June an envoy (the Achinese ambassador, who had hidden in the jungle) brought a letter in Portuguese under a flag of truce, laying the cause on de Weert's attempt to bring the king by force on board and offering peace or war as the Dutch chose; Bree gives its opening as 'God yesterday executed right and justice, and this for reasons', and a second reply, to the Dutch answer carried by a freed Portuguese slave woman, as 'God does justice to those that ask justice of him, and that deserve it from him'. Two wounded boatswains were recovered on 3 June, one carried to the shore in a mat by two villagers who ran off 'so that they might not be recognized'. The ships' council refused the king's later excuses of 'misunderstanding on both sides'. Seventy years later Philippus Baldaeus (1672) tells it with the king's ambassador warning of a plot to seize him aboard, a council deliberation, de Weert 'somewhat heated with strong liquor' saying the empress 'could not be in distress for a man', the king saying 'Bind the dog' as he left the room, de Weert's head split with a scimitar, the order for the rest relayed through the prince of Uva, one boy, Isaac Plevier, surviving, and the letter 'Who drinks wine is not good: God shews his justice: If you desire peace, you shall have peace; if war, war'; he then gives the king's burning fever, his reported view that de Weert 'had no more than what he deserved', and his death in 1604.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C007's sources refuse the one exception almost everyone makes: the hatred felt in killing an enemy who comes to harm you is, Margaya says, the fierce form of the hate-rooted mind [C007-M:L11], and the digest records that the sources make no exception for justified anger. Here the claim of that exception survives in the claimant's own letter of the next morning, 'God yesterday executed right and justice'. The texts also split the hate-rooted minds only by urging [C007-P:L25–L28; C007-M:L9], and the accounts divide on exactly that: an order after an answer (Bree), a king urged by his own people (Rycks), a whisper and a council (Baldaeus). And the texts' ordinary occasions [C007-M:L17] fit both parties: each had asked the other for something and been refused. The place binds because the story can only be located, as the documents locate it, from the ships' side, along a bearing: the camera stands where every writer stood.
what_is_certain: The Dutch fleet under de Weert anchored in an open roadstead off 'Matecalo' on 25 April 1603; Bree and Rycks agree on the date and Ferguson notes there was 'no harbour where the Dutch ships lay, only an open roadstead' (JCBRAS XXXI, 1928, pp. 134, 158–159, 170).

Rycks's sailing direction: 'a dangerous shore, so that one can with difficulty see where the roadstead is, because Matekelo lies a short mile inland. But there is a mountain inland, that we call Hang Up. When this is between west and west-by-north of you, then you are in the roadstead, and one lies there in 7 and 8 or 9 fathoms water, excellent bottom, fine sand' (Ferguson, p. 170).

Ferguson identifies Hang Up with the peak later called Capello de Frade, Nunnikskap and Friar's Hood, notes that 'from Karativu looking inland Friar's Hood lies west by north', identifies the 1603 town of Matecalo with Sammanthurai 'between three and four miles from the sea', and the sources' 'river of Poligamme' with the northern entrance of the backwater, 28 to 30 miles from Karativu (pp. 106–107 n. 15; 134 n. 29; 158–159 n. 98; 170 nn. 3–5).

On 1 June 1603 de Weert went ashore with about 200 men (Bree and Rycks both give 200), met Vimaladharmasuriya I near Matecalo, stayed with a small party when the rest were sent back, and was killed with a number of his men (Ferguson, pp. 146–149, 175–177).

The earliest account to reach Europe is the 'Discourse' compiled from papers received in Holland on 17 March 1604 and printed by P. A. Tiele in 1883; it gives the refused invitation, de Weert's reply that he would sail home, an order to 'the Modlear, a Portuguese renegado, to bind the vice-admiral and thereafter to kill him and all other Dutch', 'the vice-admiral and about 49 men besides' killed, and the fleet's surmise that the true cause was the release of the Portuguese (Ferguson, pp. 122–124).

A letter in Portuguese in the king's name reached the ships under a flag of truce on 2 June, laying the cause on de Weert's attempt to bring the king by force on board and offering peace or war; Bree gives its opening as 'God yesterday executed right and justice, and this for reasons' (Ferguson, pp. 148–149).

The king had written before the killing asking that the Portuguese prisoners not be released, and de Weert released them on 29 May with passports, on a promise given at their capture (Bree, Ferguson pp. 145–146).
Every surviving account is from the Dutch or Portuguese side; the king's words survive only as quoted, in translation, by the recipients.

Sammanthurai, the Karaitivu shore and the Friar's Hood triangulation station all lie in Ampara District (Nominatim reverse geocodes at zoom 10 and 16; Survey Department station listed in the Uhana division).
what_is_disputed: Where it happened. Modern summaries (Wikipedia, the Atlas of Mutual Heritage, popular sites) say 'Batticaloa', meaning the later fort-town on the backwater; the 1603 accounts as read by Ferguson put the town several miles inland of the southern coast, at present Sammanthurai. The distance inland is itself given three ways: 'a short mile' (Rycks), 'some full two miles' (Bree), and Ferguson's three to four English miles; Ferguson's identification is an inference from these and from the bearing, and the landing village is only 'perhaps Karativu'. The spot of the king's lodging ('an enclosed garden where stood a number of huts and houses', Rycks) is unknown.

How many died. 'The vice-admiral and about 49 men besides' (Discourse, Bree); 'up to some 50 persons' (the king's letter as Bree reports it); 47, with six wounded who recovered (Rycks); all 53 (the Spilbergen diarist, per Ferguson); 'scarce any one ... except a boy' plus some swimmers (Baldaeus). The widely repeated 'about 300 men ... on the beach' (Wikipedia, citing de Silva and Beumer 1988, not read here) cannot be right on the primary counts, since only about 200 landed and most regained the ships; 300 is the number both diaries give for armed men on the king's side.

Why it happened. The refused invitation and de Weert's reply (Discourse, Bree); the released Portuguese prisoners (fleet opinion in the Discourse and Bree; Rycks; Baldaeus); drink and mutual abuse (Rycks; Ferguson adds a Portuguese captain, Antonio Martins, not read here); a warning of a plot to seize the king aboard (Baldaeus). Bree says nothing of drink; that is silence, not denial.

Whether anyone urged the order. None in the Discourse and Bree (an order after an answer); 'his people, who incited him, so that he consented' (Rycks); the ambassador's whisper and a council's deliberation (Baldaeus).

The words. 'Bind the dog' and the remark that the empress 'could not be in distress for a man' are in Baldaeus (1672) only; the 1603 accounts have an order to bind without the insult. A Sinhala form of the order quoted online ('Bandapan mé balla') could not be traced to any source read here.

The letter. Bree: 'God yesterday executed right and justice, and this for reasons', and 'God does justice to those that ask justice of him, and that deserve it from him'. Baldaeus: 'Que bebem vinho, noa he bon. Deos fes justitia; se quesieres pas, pas; se quires guerra, guerra' (as printed in 1732), written, he says, after the king reached Kandy. These are different letters or different memories; neither is the original, and Bree's reaches English through a German translation.

Baldaeus's sequel: the king's burning fever, the cold brook, his reported lament over the killing, his reported view that de Weert 'had no more than what he deserved', and his death in 1604. Recorded here so the passage is not told halfway; it is uncorroborated in the 1603 sources read here and is excluded from the film on the kamma floor.

Which peak is Hang Up. Ferguson's identification with Friar's Hood rests on the bearing from Karaitivu; this record's own check (Friar's Hood triangulation station at about 7°26'N 81°30'E, a rounded coordinate) gives about 279 degrees from the Karaitivu shore, inside Rycks's 'between west and west-by-north', but the summit's exact position and height (658 m in one travel source) are not surveyed here.
sources: Donald Ferguson, 'The Earliest Dutch Visits to Ceylon', Journal of the Ceylon Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society vol. XXXI no. 81 (1928): Annexure C (de Weert's letters), D1 (the 1604 Discourse, from P. A. Tiele, Bijdragen en Mededeelingen van het Historisch Genootschap 6, 1883), D2 (Bree's diary, from de Bry 1605/1606), D3 (Rycks's journal, Hague archives)

what_to_film: Sea end, evening: a drone locked about 100–120 m over the surf at the Karaitivu shore, facing inland on a bearing of about 279 degrees, longest lens: surf, palm fringe, plain, and Friar's Hood on the horizon; repeat on several evenings for the peak's silhouette and on the alignment evening for the sun setting into it.
Sea end, dawn: a locked wide frame at the tideline looking out along the reverse bearing (about 99 degrees) toward the anchorage, the sun rising out of the sea to one side.

The plain: from a raised field bund west of Sammanthurai, on the bearing, a very long lens held through the morning as the heat haze rises and erases the peak; then locked details on the same line (a straight channel, a bund edge, the shimmer).
The backwater arm between the coast strip and the fields, late afternoon, looking west along the bearing, the peak doubled in still water.

Inland end, pre-dawn: from the summit of Friar's Hood (or, failing access, the highest reachable point on its eastern flank), locked, looking east along the bearing over the plain to the sea's edge as first light comes.
Sound: surf at the sea end, wind at the summit; no music, no ambient town sound.
suggested_location.access: The sea end is a public beach; a drone over the surf needs Civil Aviation Authority of Sri Lanka registration and permission, and on this coast the Ministry of Defence clearance that accompanies it; the security forces maintain camps in the district and a recce should confirm there is no restricted zone on the line. A boat position offshore is a fallback if the drone is refused, but from a boat the palm fringe may hide all but the top of the peak. The plain is private paddy land reached by farm tracks; filming from bunds needs the owners' leave. Friar's Hood lies in the Nuwaragala forest reserve: a Forest Department permit is needed, the approaches (via Bandaraduwa or Mangalagama) are rough tracks, the reserve is elephant country, and a local guide is essential; a pre-dawn summit shot means a night on or near the peak. None of this has been verified.
suggested_location.best_time: The south-west monsoon months, May to September, are this coast's dry season and give the clearest evenings. The sunset alignment from the Karaitivu shore should fall, on this record's calculation from a rounded coordinate (bearing about 279 degrees, solar declination about +8.9 degrees), around 28–29 August and 13–14 April; the true dates may differ by several days and must be fixed with an ephemeris and a surveyed summit position before the shoot. Late August is preferred (dry season; April is the stormier inter-monsoon). Evenings for the sea end, dawn for the summit; mid-morning only for the haze sequence.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, 26 September 2026, done blind to this record's previous body. The primary accounts were read in Donald Ferguson's translations and notes in JCBRAS vol. XXXI no. 81 (1928), from the archive.org OCR (in.ernet.dli.2015.104403): the 1604 Discourse (pp. 122–125), Bree's diary (pp. 125–159) and Rycks's journal (pp. 170–177). Baldaeus was read in the English of Churchill's Collection vol. III (1732), pp. 610–611, from the archive.org OCR. Not read: Wieder's 1933 Linschoten-Vereeniging edition of the Spilbergen voyage, the Dutch and German originals, Commelin's Begin ende Voortgangh, the Portuguese account of Antonio Martins, Queyroz, Couto, and Ferguson's later annexures (F5, G3), which were not in the scan; nor any Sinhala chronicle, so no claim is made that the island's own chronicles are silent. Corrections to the blind proposal: (1) place (failure mode 4, a similar name): the proposal's lagoon mouth and beach at the north of the backwater is the sources' 'river of Poligamme', some 30 miles from the anchorage; the 1603 Matecalo lay inland of the southern coast, which moves the film from Batticaloa to Ampara District. (2) The '300 on the beach' (failure mode 3) cannot be reconciled with about 200 landed. (3) 'Bind the dog', the drink on de Weert's side only and the queen remark are Baldaeus's (1672); the proposal presented them as the story, and they are one layer of four (failure mode 2). (4) The proposal gave only Baldaeus's letter; Bree's earlier wording differs (failure mode 8), and Baldaeus's passage continues with the king's fever and a 'deserved', which is why the film cannot take it whole and does not take it at all. (5) Bree's silence on drink is not a denial (failure mode 6). (6) The proposal's payoff, a static high frame of a lagoon bar, repeats IDEA-0147. District: every point on the line reverse-geocodes to Ampara District (Nominatim, zoom 10: the Karaitivu shore at 7.377, 81.856 and the Friar's Hood station at 7.4333, 81.50; zoom 16 on the shore returns Beach Road, Karaitivu); Sammanthurai geocodes to 7.370, 81.812 in the same district. Budget: Ampara stood at 5 on the slate without GRP-02 and GRP-03 (IDEA-0056, IDEA-0075, IDEA-0076, IDEA-0124, IDEA-0159) and neither blind selection placed a film there, so this takes it to 6, above the preferred 4 and below the closed 7; the reason is that this is where the story happened, and the proposal's district (Batticaloa, which stays at 4) holds no part of it. Coordinates are the shore at the sea end of the line; the bearing and the 40 km distance are this record's arithmetic from the rounded GeoNames coordinate of the Friar's Hood triangulation station (the station's listed elevation of 73 m is a gazetteer artefact; one travel source gives the peak 658 m). The sunset dates are this record's calculation and are unverified. Images: Commons holds nothing for Friar's Hood, Walimbe Hela, Nuwaragala or the Karaitivu shore; one confirmed photograph of the Sammanthurai plain is carried and captioned as not the bearing. The 1605 de Bry engravings of the reception and the killing exist (one is on Commons as RP-P-OB-75.430) but are not used, as the film uses no archival images. Fallback in a different district, not researched here: the blind selector's Negombo lagoon mouth (Gampaha) for the missing clause of the 1638 treaty.

unknowns: Whether the inland peak is visible from a legal drone height over the surf at the sea end on dry-season evenings, and how often haze hides it.
The surveyed position and height of the summit, and therefore the true bearing and the true sunset-alignment dates.

Forest Department access to the summit, the route, and whether a pre-dawn ascent is safe in elephant country.
What Wieder's 1933 edition, the Dutch originals and the Portuguese accounts add or contradict, especially on the place and on the letter's wording.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was proposed by Claude on 2026-09-26 and awaits Chathura's review; no verdict has been given. The historical accounts are quoted from Ferguson's published English translations and from the 1732 English Baldaeus; the identification of the 1603 anchorage and town is Ferguson's inference, and the bearing and alignment dates are this record's own arithmetic. Everything about access, visibility and permissions is desk research and unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
